tier_reason: The README 'Key features' list states verbatim '4x faster than ttx on CFF OTF, and 40x on TTF' and '900x faster than makeotf for building a fully-optimized CFF OTF', with no fonts, hardware, compiler, flags, tool versions or timing method, and no benchmark script in the repo (tests/ holds cffdump-opcode-check.js, ttf-roundtrip-test.js and payload/). First-party numbers without methodology are tier C; the 900x row would also hit the >50x unstated-flags cap.

corrections.caveats: First-party README claim only: no hardware, font files, font sizes, tool versions, run counts, compiler or flags are given, and the visible tests directory (cffdump-opcode-check.js, ttf-roundtrip-test.js, payload) holds correctness checks, not a benchmark (the github.com listing was truncated, so a hidden timing script cannot be fully ruled out). otfccdump has a --time flag that times substeps, so the claim is easy to re-measure but nobody published such a run. ttx is a Python tool (fontTools), so the 4x and 40x rows are C against Python, not C against another C/C++ implementation; makeotf is Adobe's AFDKO build tool and probably takes different input than otfccbuild, so the build job may not be identical (inference, not stated in the README); the README does not say which -O level the 900x build used, and a 900x gain with unstated method is implausible enough to cap it at C on its own. Undated numbers; both baselines have changed since the repo was archived (2022-06-04). Web search snippets (typedrawers.com forum posts by the author, page not opened) say early TrueType-only builds parsed a 26 MB Chinese TTF in about 10 s versus about 10 min for ttx and built a 24 MB font in about 6 s versus about 4 min for ttx; snippet only, not used for the tier. Security: several 2022 fuzzing CVEs report heap buffer overflows in otfccdump (CVE-2022-35035 at commit 617837b, CVE-2022-35448 and CVE-2022-35463 at v0.10.4, CVSS 6.5, public PoCs in github.com/Cvjark/Poc); they were published after the repo was archived, so they are presumably unfixed upstream (snippet only from osv.dev/tenable search results, advisories not opened). Do not feed untrusted fonts to otfccdump. Category fit is loose: otfcc is an OpenType serializer/compiler (font file tooling), not a shaping or layout engine. Bundled third-party code under dep/ was not audited for licences.

notes: README numbers match the record verbatim; metadata confirmed on github.com (Apache-2.0, 435 stars, 69 forks, not a fork, archived by owner Jun 4 2022, last commit Jun 3 2022 'Merge pull request #70'). Shortcomings to record: first-party claim without methodology, Python baseline for the 4x/40x rows, non-identical makeotf build job for the 900x row, archived repo with unfixed 2022 otfccdump heap-overflow CVEs (snippet only), loose fit to the font-shaping category.

tier_reason: Independent (rival-authored) measurement: TinyEXR's doc/performance-vs-openexr.md with a public harness (benchmark/bench_compare.cpp, Makefile target bench-compare), AMD Ryzen 9 3950X and gcc -O3 stated, so the method is literally A-grade. Lowered to B because the doc's data are internally inconsistent (absolute MP/s differ about 2x between the 2026-08-08 table and the charts, HTJ2K encode flips from OpenEXR about 3x in the charts to TinyEXR 18.7 vs 16.4 in the table, the M1 table and M1 chart disagree), OpenEXR's HTJ2K values are carried over from an older run rather than measured in the same run, and OpenEXR is linked from an out-of-tree build ($(HOME)/work/openexr/_build) with unstated 4.0-dev commit, CMake configuration and x86 OpenJPH version, so no OpenEXR-favouring ratio ties to one reproducible run.

corrections.baseline: TinyEXR v3 (pure-C11 EXR codec by the TinyEXR author). OpenEXR's leads are against TinyEXR's dependency-free in-tree build (DEFLATE=intree, the freestanding/WASM path) and against TinyEXR's HTJ2K codec; TinyEXR's hosted default (DEFLATE=auto, vendored libdeflate 1.25, the same backend OpenEXR uses) matches or beats OpenEXR on ZIP/ZIPS/PXR24.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Mixed, rival-authored results; current pinned Ryzen 9 3950X single-thread run (README headline charts doc/perf-libdeflate-htj2k-decode.svg and -encode.svg, values also in doc/gen_perf_charts.py), MP/s TinyEXR in-tree vs OpenEXR: decode zip 32.2 vs 30.7 (TinyEXR ahead), zips 17.0 vs 24.4 (OpenEXR 1.44x), pxr24 29.9 vs 43.8 (OpenEXR 1.46x), htj2k256 23.2 vs 29.8 (OpenEXR 1.28x), htj2k32 23.5 vs 27.9 (OpenEXR 1.19x); encode zip 9.6 vs 14 (OpenEXR 1.46x), zips 10.3 vs 14.8 (1.44x), pxr24 9.2 vs 15.8 (1.72x), htj2k256 11 vs 33.2 (3.0x), htj2k32 11.6 vs 31.6 (2.7x) (all ratios derived from page data). Against TinyEXR's default libdeflate build OpenEXR is slower or tied on the deflate family (decode zip 42.4 vs 30.7, zips 31.8 vs 24.4, pxr24 43.7 vs 43.8; encode zip 15.3 vs 14, zips 16.2 vs 14.8, pxr24 16.4 vs 15.8) and keeps only HTJ2K decode (24.1 vs 29.8 and 23.5 vs 27.9, about 1.2x) and PIZ decode (33.8 vs 35.6, about 1.05x). The doc's TL;DR and the README quote older ratios from doc/perf-decode.svg (in-tree decode zip 51.2 vs 62.1 = 1.21x, zips 23.1 vs 48.7 = 2.11x, pxr24 49 vs 88.9 = 1.81x, piz 24.8 vs 67.5 = 2.72x before TinyEXR's PIZ rewrite, htj2k256 24.6 vs 59.7 = 2.43x, htj2k32 27.7 vs 55 = 1.99x; derived from page data); the README's 'HTJ2K ~2.5-3x' decode and '~4x' encode lines exceed those charts. At 16 threads (in-tree, doc/perf-mt-compare.svg) OpenEXR leads PIZ decode 207.7 vs 110.5 (1.88x) and PXR24 269.5 vs 242.1 (1.11x) while TinyEXR leads RLE/ZIP/ZIPS/B44; with libdeflate at 16 threads TinyEXR leads zip 339.6 vs 226.6 and zips 358.5 vs 151.1. TinyEXR wins uncompressed (1380 vs 389) and RLE (114 vs 45.5) decode outright.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc -O3 (doc setup line 'OpenEXR 4.0-dev, gcc -O3'; Makefile builds benchmark/bench_compare.cpp with $(CXX) -std=c++14 -O3 and bench_tx.c with -O3, TinyEXR library with V3_OPT=-O3 for the headline run although the Makefile default is -O2); compiler version not stated; OpenEXR is linked from an out-of-tree build at $(HOME)/work/openexr/_build whose commit, CMake build type and OpenJPH version (x86) are not stated. Apple M1 rows: Apple clang 21, OpenJPH 0.27.
corrections.hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3950X (16C/32T, Zen2), avx2+f16c, machine idle; secondary Apple M1 (4P+4E, macOS 26) runs
corrections.stars_or_usage: 1.9k stars, 703 forks; reference implementation of the EXR format used across film VFX tools
corrections.caveats: Evidence is a rival project's benchmark (TinyEXR author), not an OpenEXR claim, and it is mixed: OpenEXR is itself the incumbent EXR library and TinyEXR is not a default, so this entry is the reference implementation beating a lightweight alternative, and the doc's net conclusion is that TinyEXR's default hosted build (vendored libdeflate) matches or beats OpenEXR on ZIP/ZIPS/PXR24 single-thread and leads the whole deflate family at 16 threads (zip 339.6 vs 226.6, zips 358.5 vs 151.1 MP/s). OpenEXR's clear wins are HTJ2K (OpenJPH backend) and deflate-family encode/decode versus TinyEXR's dependency-free in-tree codec. The doc is internally inconsistent: the 2026-08-08 'full single-thread numbers' table reports roughly half the absolute MP/s of the charts and README text for both libraries (OpenEXR rle decode 45.5 vs 88.2, b44 86.8 vs 180.2; README uncompressed 2699 vs 789 against the doc's 1384 vs 392), the table shows TinyEXR faster on HTJ2K encode (18.7 vs 16.4) while the headline encode chart shows OpenEXR about 3x faster (33.2 vs 11), and the Apple M1 table (OpenEXR decode zips 60.6 vs 22.2, piz 66.1 vs 28.2) disagrees with the M1 chart data in doc/gen_perf_charts.py (zips 60 vs 56, piz 64 vs 68). The doc's TL;DR and the README quote stale ratios (PIZ 2.7x predates TinyEXR's PIZ rewrite, now 33.8 vs 35.6; README HTJ2K 2.5-3x decode exceeds the chart's 2.43x/1.99x). OpenEXR/OpenJPH HTJ2K values are 'the latest available same-machine baseline', not re-measured in the same run as TinyEXR's 2026-06-13 HTJ2K numbers. OpenEXR is linked from an out-of-tree build ($(HOME)/work/openexr/_build) with unstated commit and CMake options. One small 660x440 four-channel HALF image (asakusa.exr), which limits thread scaling and makes per-call overhead count. OpenEXR's own release notes (CHANGES.md 3.3, 3.5, per the search record) give only unquantified or self-relative speed claims, no outside baseline; openexr.com not opened.

notes: Benchmark page and README opened; harness (benchmark/bench_compare.cpp, Makefile bench-compare) and chart data (doc/*.svg, doc/gen_perf_charts.py) read directly, which recovered the in-tree numbers the search agent could not read. The record's TL;DR ratios are real but stale; the current pinned run shows smaller OpenEXR leads (about 1.45x ZIPS/PXR24 decode, 1.2-1.3x HTJ2K decode, 1.4-1.7x deflate-family encode, 2.7-3x HTJ2K encode vs in-tree TinyEXR) and OpenEXR losing or tying against TinyEXR's default libdeflate build. Shortcomings to record: rival-authored mixed evidence, incumbent measured against a non-default alternative, internally inconsistent doc data, HTJ2K baseline not same-run, out-of-tree OpenEXR build with unstated commit; metadata confirmed (BSD-3-Clause, 1.9k stars, 703 forks, last commit Oct 10 2026, active).
